01895bfd.text: Immanuel Kant, 1724 to 1804. Kant's view contrasts sharply with utilitarianism. For him, the only thing good without qualification is a good will. That's a will that acts because something is right, not because of how it turns out. Morality, then, is about acting from duty. Consequences do not decide what is right, not even saving your friends. The principle behind your act does.
01895bfd.spoken: Immanuel Kant, 1724 to 1804. Kant's view contrasts sharply with utilitarianism. For him, the only thing good without qualification is a good will. That's a will that acts because something is right, not because of how it turns out. Morality, then, is about acting from duty. Consequences do not decide what is right, not even saving your friends. The principle behind your act does.

f5f37bf3.text: Why you do it matters. Kant draws a sharp line between two motives that can produce the very same action. First, acting from duty, because it's right. You protect your friends because you recognize protecting them as the right thing to do. This has genuine moral worth for Kant. It would hold even if you did not feel like it. Second, acting from inclination, because you feel like it. You protect them only because you love them and it feels good. That's kind and lovely, but Kant says it carries no distinctively moral worth on its own.

6538d5e0.text: So the real question isn't, what happens if I lie? It's, what am I willing to make a law for everyone?

38090da2.text: Two kinds of ought. Commands come in two flavors, and only one is the home of morality. A hypothetical imperative commands a means to an end you happen to want. If you want to stay safe, keep quiet. Drop the want, and the command vanishes. A categorical imperative commands unconditionally. It binds any rational being, wants or no wants. Do not lie, with no if. This, Kant says, is the form of a genuine moral law.

2bb07612.text: Right. A hypothetical imperative commands a means to an end you happen to want. A categorical imperative commands unconditionally, whatever you want.

c19947af.text: Formulation one: universal law. The categorical imperative has one core, stated several ways. The first goes like this. Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law. In short, could you will that everyone act on your maxim? If universalizing it breaks something, it fails. This is not the Golden Rule. Kant himself said the Golden Rule could not serve as the moral law. It turns on what you would want done to you. His test holds whatever you want.

1b1953d2.text: Two ways a maxim can fail. The machine flagged two different failures, and the difference between them defines two kinds of duty. First, a contradiction in conception. You can't even imagine it. Universalizing the maxim makes it self-destruct, as with lying and false promises. This yields a perfect duty: strict, with no exceptions. Do not lie. Second, a contradiction in the will. You can't rationally want it. You can picture the world, but couldn't rationally will it, as when no one ever helps. This yields an imperfect duty: real, but you choose how and when. Help others sometimes.

82a97d66.text: Who gets to be an end? Kant's respect is owed to a specific class. He calls them persons: rational beings capable of setting their own ends and acting on reasons.

51344b95.text: Kant bites the bullet. This case is really Kant's. In 1797, in On a Supposed Right to Lie, he answered the writer Benjamin Constant. Constant objected: surely you may lie to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding.

e5f4ce45.text: Korsgaard: dealing with evil. In The Right to Lie: Kant on Dealing with Evil, from 1986, Korsgaard argues that Kant's own test, applied honestly to the situation, gives a different answer. First, orthodox Kant: never lie. Truthfulness is unconditional. Even to the cat, you may not lie, as in the 1797 essay. You answer for your lie. What the cat does with the truth is his affair. Now Korsgaard, on dealing with evil. Ideal rules assume everyone complies. The cat does not comply. He is using coercion to do murder. A maxim like, deceive a deceiver to thwart violence, can be universalized. You needn't cooperate with his evil. The Universal Law formula can permit the lie.

72695e50.text: And the real mouse? Korsgaard also reopens who counts. In Fellow Creatures, from 2018, she argues Kant got animals wrong. First, Kant: indirect duties only. Animals aren't rational, so they're not ends in themselves. We owe them only indirect duties. A real mouse at your door? On Kant's view, no standing of its own. Now Korsgaard, on fellow creatures. Creatures for whom things can be good or bad are ends in themselves too, so we owe them direct duties. The real mouse counts in its own right. So, for that matter, would the cat.
